templates.pattern: A binary search is performed on a sorted list of [N] items. Calculate the maximum number of comparisons needed.
templates.explanation:
Binary search max comparisons = log₂(n+1)
= log₂([N]+1)
= log₂([N+1])
= [RESULT]

Binary search halves the search space with each comparison. For n = 2^k − 1 items it takes exactly k comparisons. This is O(log n) — far more efficient than linear search for large lists.

templates.pattern: A merge sort is applied to a list of [N] items where N is a power of 2. Calculate the recursion depth of the merge sort.
templates.explanation:
Merge sort recursion depth = log₂(n)
= log₂([N])
= [RESULT]

Each level of recursion halves the list size. A list of 1024 items requires 10 levels of recursion. This depth also equals the number of merge phases needed.

templates.pattern: A hash table has a size of [SIZE] slots. A key with value [KEY] is inserted. Calculate the hash index using the formula: key mod table size.
templates.explanation:
Hash index = key mod table size
= [KEY] mod [SIZE]
= [KEY] % [SIZE]
= [RESULT]

Hash tables use modulo arithmetic to map keys to array positions. Prime number table sizes reduce clustering and improve distribution of keys.

templates.pattern: A hash table has [SIZE] slots and currently stores [ITEMS] items. Calculate the load factor of the hash table.
templates.explanation:
Load factor = items ÷ table size
= [ITEMS] ÷ [SIZE]
= [RESULT]

A load factor above 0.7 causes too many collisions and degrades performance. When the load factor exceeds the threshold the table is resized — typically doubled.

templates.pattern: A hash table has [SIZE] slots and [ITEMS] items are inserted. Assuming perfect distribution calculate the number of collisions.
templates.explanation:
Collisions = items − table size (when items > size)
= [ITEMS] − [SIZE]
= [RESULT]

A collision occurs when two keys hash to the same index. Collisions are handled by chaining (linked lists at each slot) or open addressing (probing for next free slot).

templates.pattern: A binary search is performed on a sorted list of [N] items. After [K] comparisons how many items remain in the search range?
templates.explanation:
Remaining items = n ÷ 2^k
= [N] ÷ 2^[K]
= [N] ÷ [pow(2,K)]
= [RESULT]

Each binary search comparison halves the remaining search space. After k comparisons the remaining range is n/2^k items.

templates.pattern: A merge sort is applied to a list of [N] items where N is a power of 2. Calculate the total number of comparisons in the worst case.
templates.explanation:
Merge sort total comparisons = n × log₂(n)
= [N] × log₂([N])
= [N] × [log2(N)]
= [RESULT]

Merge sort has O(n log n) time complexity in all cases — best, average and worst. This makes it more efficient than O(n²) algorithms like bubble sort for large lists.

templates.pattern: A breadth-first search tree has a branching factor of 2. Calculate the number of nodes at level [K] of the tree.
templates.explanation:
Nodes at level k = 2^k (for binary tree)
= 2^[K]
= [RESULT]

In a BFS tree with branching factor b, level k has b^k nodes. The total nodes up to level k grows exponentially — this is why BFS can be memory-intensive for deep searches.

templates.pattern: In a weighted graph Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from source to destination through nodes with edge weights [W1], [W2] and [W3]. Calculate the total path cost.
templates.explanation:
Total path cost = sum of edge weights along path
= [W1] + [W2] + [W3]
= [RESULT]

Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. It uses a priority queue to always process the lowest-cost node next.

templates.pattern: An algorithm processes [N] operations. Each operation takes [R] microseconds. Calculate the total execution time in microseconds.
templates.explanation:
Total time = number of operations × time per operation
= [N] × [R]
= [RESULT] microseconds

This is the basis of time complexity analysis. If doubling n doubles the time the algorithm is O(n). If it quadruples the time it is O(n²).
